topFixes.title: Hard-coded Stripe live key
topFixes.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

topFixes.title: Environment file committed: .env
topFixes.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.

topFixes.title: JWTs accepted with the "none" algorithm
topFixes.recommendation: Always verify tokens with an explicit algorithm allow-list, and check exp, aud and iss. Use decode only for logging-free inspection of already-verified tokens.

topFixes.title: Untrusted PR code checked out in a privileged workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
topFixes.recommendation: Use the pull_request trigger for anything that builds or tests PR code. Keep pull_request_target for labelling or commenting, without checking out the head.

topFixes.title: Publicly accessible database: aws_db_instance.main
topFixes.recommendation: Turn off public accessibility, place the database in private subnets, and reach it through the application, a bastion or a private endpoint.

findings.title: Untrusted PR code checked out in a privileged workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
findings.observed: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs on pull_request_target and references the pull request head at line 10.
findings.expected: Workflows triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run do not check out or run code from the pull request.
findings.risk: These triggers run with secrets and a write token. Checking out the PR head lets anyone who opens a pull request run code with them ("pwn request").
findings.recommendation: Use the pull_request trigger for anything that builds or tests PR code. Keep pull_request_target for labelling or commenting, without checking out the head.
findings.example:
on: pull_request          # untrusted code, no secrets, read-only token
permissions:
  contents: read

findings.title: Environment file committed: .env
findings.observed: .env is tracked by git and assigns 3 variable(s). Secret-looking variables: DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. Values are not shown.
findings.expected: Environment files with real values stay out of version control. Only templates such as .env.example are committed, and .gitignore excludes .env files.
findings.risk: A committed .env file usually holds live credentials, which are then exposed to everyone with repository access and remain in git history.
findings.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.
findings.example:
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

findings.title: Hard-coded Stripe live key

findings.title: No incident response plan
findings.observed: No incident response plan was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: An incident response plan defines roles, severity levels, escalation paths and how internal and external communication happens.

## Roles
Incident lead: on-call engineer. Comms: head of support.
## Severity
SEV1: data exposure or full outage. SEV2: partial outage. SEV3: minor.

findings.title: No reliable backups for aws_db_instance.main

findings.recommendation: Enable encryption at rest on every data store (it usually requires a replacement for existing RDS instances: snapshot, copy encrypted, restore).

findings.title: Trackers load without a consent check

findings.recommendation: Load trackers only after the visitor opts in (a consent manager or your own gate), default to opted-out, and honour navigator.globalPrivacyControl.

posthog.init(KEY, { opt_out_capturing_by_default: true });
if (consent.analytics && !navigator.globalPrivacyControl) posthog.opt_in_capturing();

findings.title: No CODEOWNERS file

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Leaked deploy key | Low | High | @platform | Mitigate: OIDC, no stored keys |

## Assets
Customer PII in Postgres; API keys for payment providers.

Public API, admin console, webhook endpoint.

| Threat | Mitigation |

findings.expected: A secret scanner runs on every push or pull request (and ideally as a pre-commit hook), with push protection enabled on the hosting platform.
findings.risk: Without automated scanning, a committed credential is found by an attacker before it is found by you.
findings.recommendation: Add Gitleaks (or TruffleHog) to CI and to pre-commit, and enable GitHub secret scanning with push protection.
findings.example:
# .github/workflows/secrets.yml
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  gitleaks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@<sha>

findings.title: No offboarding procedure
findings.observed: No offboarding procedure was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: Offboarding revokes SSO, source control, cloud, CI/CD and vendor access within a set deadline (≤ 24h).
findings.risk: Departed staff and contractors keep working credentials, a common source of incidents and an audit finding.
findings.recommendation: Document an offboarding checklist covering every system with access, and the deadline for completing it.
findings.example:
## Offboarding (within 24 hours)
- [ ] Disable SSO account (cascades to apps via SCIM)
- [ ] Remove from GitHub org and npm org
- [ ] Revoke personal cloud credentials and tokens

findings.title: Token issued without an expiry
findings.observed: A token is signed in src/auth.js at line 12 with no expiry nearby.
findings.expected: Every token the application issues has an expiry, so access ends even if revocation fails.
findings.risk: A token without expiry stays valid forever; one leak is permanent access.
findings.recommendation: Set a short expiry on every issued token and use refresh tokens that can be revoked.
findings.example: jwt.sign(claims, key, { algorithm: 'RS256', expiresIn: '15m' });

findings.title: No HTTP security headers configured
findings.observed: HTTP server or web framework detected in package.json, but no security-headers middleware or CSP/HSTS configuration was found in code or config. They may be set at a CDN; if so, add an exception that says where.
findings.expected: Responses set CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options and frame protections, in code or at the edge (CDN, proxy, platform config).
findings.risk: Missing headers remove browser-side defences against XSS, clickjacking and protocol downgrade.
findings.recommendation: Add a security-headers middleware (helmet, Talisman, SecurityMiddleware) or set the headers in your proxy or platform configuration.
findings.example:
import helmet from 'helmet';
app.use(helmet({ hsts: { maxAge: 31536000, includeSubDomains: true } }));

findings.title: DOM innerHTML/outerHTML assigned without visible sanitization
findings.observed: DOM innerHTML/outerHTML assigned without visible sanitization in src/public/app.js at line 2.
findings.expected: HTML output is escaped by the framework; raw-HTML sinks are avoided or fed only sanitized content.
findings.risk: Rendering raw HTML that contains user input enables cross-site scripting: session theft and actions on the victim's behalf.
findings.recommendation: Render text through the framework's escaping. Where raw HTML is unavoidable, sanitize it with DOMPurify (or bleach) on the same line so the intent is visible.
findings.example: <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(html) }} />

findings.title: Plain HTTP URL to api.partner-service.com
findings.observed: http://api.partner-service.com is used in src/server.js at line 37.
findings.expected: Every external and internal service URL uses https://. Plain HTTP is limited to localhost and documentation examples.
findings.risk: Requests over plain HTTP can be read and modified in transit, including tokens and personal data.
findings.recommendation: Switch the URL to https:// and make sure the target service redirects HTTP to HTTPS with HSTS.
findings.example: const API_URL = process.env.API_URL ?? 'https://api.example.com';

findings.title: Unpinned base image node:latest
findings.observed: node:latest in Dockerfile at line 1 has no version tag or uses :latest.
findings.expected: Base images use an explicit version tag, ideally pinned by digest, from a trusted registry.
findings.risk: An untagged or :latest base image changes underneath you, so builds are not reproducible and a compromised upstream image flows straight in.
findings.recommendation: Pin base images to a version and digest, and let Dependabot or Renovate propose updates.
findings.example: FROM node:22.11.0-bookworm-slim@sha256:<digest>

findings.title: Container images are not scanned
findings.observed: The repository builds container images but no image scanner (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Docker Scout) runs in CI.
findings.expected: Images built from this repository are scanned (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Docker Scout) before they are pushed or deployed.
findings.risk: Base images and OS packages carry their own vulnerabilities that dependency scanning of your code does not see.
findings.recommendation: Scan each built image in CI and fail on Critical/High vulnerabilities with a fix available.
findings.example:
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
  with: { image-ref: 'app:${{ github.sha }}', severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH', exit-code: '1', ignore-unfixed: true }

findings.title: `npm install` used in a build
findings.observed: Dockerfile runs npm install at line 4; use npm ci to install from the lockfile.
findings.expected: Builds install exactly what the lockfile says (npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, pip --require-hashes).
findings.risk: `npm install` in CI can rewrite the lockfile and pull versions nobody reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Use the lockfile-respecting install command in CI and Dockerfiles.
findings.example:
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
# or
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prod

findings.title: Container runs as root: Dockerfile
findings.observed: Dockerfile never sets a non-root USER in its final stage.
findings.expected: The final stage of each Dockerfile switches to a non-root USER.
findings.risk: A process running as root turns any code execution bug into full control of the container and an easier escape to the host.
findings.recommendation: Create or use an unprivileged user and switch to it in the final stage.
findings.example:
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --ingroup app app
USER app

findings.title: No continuous vulnerability monitoring
findings.observed: Neither Dependabot/Renovate nor a scheduled dependency scan is configured.
findings.expected: New vulnerabilities in existing dependencies are detected continuously (Dependabot/Renovate alerts or a scheduled scan).
findings.risk: Code that does not change still becomes vulnerable as CVEs are published; without monitoring nobody finds out.
findings.recommendation: Enable Dependabot (with security updates) or Renovate, or run a dependency scan on a weekly schedule.
findings.example:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }

findings.title: No alert rules defined in code
findings.observed: No alert definitions (Prometheus rules, CloudWatch alarms, Datadog monitors, ...) were found.
findings.expected: Alerts for auth-failure spikes, error rates and infrastructure anomalies are defined as code and routed to on-call.
findings.risk: Attacks and outages that nobody is alerted to run for hours or days.
findings.recommendation: Define alert rules in code (Prometheus, CloudWatch, Datadog, Grafana) with routing to an on-call channel.

findings.title: Personal data field passed to a logger
findings.observed: Personal data field passed to a logger in public/tracking.js at line 12.
findings.expected: Logs identify people by internal id, never by email, phone, address, date of birth or IP-linked profile data.
findings.risk: Personal data in logs is copied to log platforms and backups with long retention, outside deletion and access-request processes.
findings.recommendation: Log a pseudonymous user id instead, and configure logger redaction for personal fields.
findings.example: log.info({ userId: user.id }, 'signup complete');

findings.title: No severity and triage criteria
findings.observed: No severity and triage criteria was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: Documented criteria say how a security event is classified, at what severity it becomes an incident, and how the triage outcome is recorded.
findings.risk: Without shared criteria, the same alert is ignored by one person and escalated by another, and real incidents are missed.
findings.recommendation: Document severity levels with examples, the threshold for declaring an incident, and where triage outcomes (true/false positive) are recorded.
findings.example:
| Severity | Criteria | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Confirmed data exposure or active exploitation | Leaked production key used by a third party |
Triage outcome (true/false positive, incident yes/no) is recorded on the ticket.

findings.title: No runbook for credential leak, data exposure, compromised dependency, outage or DDoS
findings.observed: Runbooks found for 0 of 4 common scenarios; missing: credential leak, data exposure, compromised dependency, outage or DDoS.
findings.expected: Runbooks cover credential leaks, data exposure, compromised dependencies and outages/DDoS.
findings.risk: Improvising the first steps of a credential leak or supply-chain incident costs the hours that matter most.
findings.recommendation: Add a short runbook per scenario: how to detect it, contain it, eradicate it and who to tell.
findings.example:
## Credential leak
1. Revoke the credential at the provider.
2. Search logs for use since the leak.
3. Rotate dependent secrets and record the incident.

findings.title: No key rotation procedure
findings.observed: No key rotation procedure was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A procedure says which secrets and keys are rotated, how, on what schedule, and on exposure or personnel change.
findings.risk: Unrotated credentials stay valid long after they leak or their holder leaves.
findings.recommendation: Document each secret, where it lives, how to rotate it, and when (≤ 90 days, or on exposure or departure).
findings.example:
## Rotating secrets
| Secret | Where | How | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Database password | AWS Secrets Manager | Automatic rotation Lambda | Every 30 days |

findings.title: Sensitive paths have no code owners
findings.observed: 5 sensitive files exist but there is no CODEOWNERS file.
findings.expected: Security-sensitive paths (auth, IAM, crypto, payments, infrastructure, workflows, migrations, lockfiles) have a specific CODEOWNERS entry, not just the catch-all.
findings.risk: Changes to the riskiest code can be approved by any reviewer instead of the people accountable for it.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit CODEOWNERS entries for sensitive paths and require code owner review. Adjust what counts as sensitive with sensitivePaths in threesock.yaml.
findings.example:
/src/auth/            @your-org/security
/infra/               @your-org/platform
/.github/workflows/   @your-org/platform

findings.title: Migration without a down step
findings.observed: migrations/001_init.up.sql has no matching 001_init.down.sql.
findings.expected: Each migration has a down/downgrade step, or the repository documents how schema changes are rolled back.
findings.risk: A bad migration without a way back turns a deploy rollback into a data-recovery incident.
findings.recommendation: Write a down migration for each change, or document the expand/contract and restore procedure used instead.
findings.example:
-- 20261022_add_status.down.sql
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status;

findings.title: Migration without a down step
findings.observed: migrations/002_customers.up.sql has no matching 002_customers.down.sql.
findings.expected: Each migration has a down/downgrade step, or the repository documents how schema changes are rolled back.
findings.risk: A bad migration without a way back turns a deploy rollback into a data-recovery incident.
findings.recommendation: Write a down migration for each change, or document the expand/contract and restore procedure used instead.
findings.example:
-- 20261022_add_status.down.sql
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status;

findings.title: No business continuity / disaster recovery plan
findings.observed: No business continuity / disaster recovery plan was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A BC/DR plan lists critical dependencies and their fallbacks, how the system is recovered, and what happens in a provider or regional outage.
findings.risk: A provider outage or loss of a key component turns into an improvised, extended outage.
findings.recommendation: Write a short continuity plan: critical dependencies, what degrades gracefully, recovery steps, and who decides.
findings.example:
## Critical dependencies
| Dependency | If unavailable |
|---|---|
| Auth provider | Existing sessions continue; new logins fail with a status banner |
## Recovery
Rebuild from IaC in the secondary region; restore the latest snapshot.

findings.title: Missing a third-party services inventory and an SBOM
findings.observed: No a third-party services inventory and an SBOM was found.
findings.expected: An inventory lists third-party services and integrations (with the data they receive), and an SBOM covers open-source dependencies.
findings.risk: Unknown vendors and SDKs receive data nobody approved, and a vendor breach cannot be assessed quickly.
findings.recommendation: Keep a third-party inventory (service, purpose, data shared, owner) and generate an SBOM in CI.
findings.example:
| Service | Purpose | Data shared | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stripe | Payments | Name, email, card token | @billing |

findings.title: Containers without resource limits in k8s/deployment.yaml
findings.observed: No resources.limits for: api.
findings.expected: Every container and task declares CPU and memory limits (and requests where the scheduler uses them).
findings.risk: One runaway workload can starve its neighbours and take down unrelated services.
findings.recommendation: Set requests and limits on every container, and memory/CPU on every task definition or compose service.

findings.title: No deletion protection on aws_db_instance.main
findings.observed: aws_db_instance.main does not set deletion_protection (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Production databases enable deletion protection so a mistaken apply or console click cannot drop them.
findings.risk: One bad `terraform apply` or a compromised credential deletes the database outright.
findings.recommendation: Enable deletion protection on databases (and turn it off deliberately when decommissioning).

findings.title: No probes in k8s/deployment.yaml
findings.observed: k8s/deployment.yaml defines a workload without readiness or liveness probes.
findings.expected: Every workload declares liveness/readiness probes (or a HEALTHCHECK / load balancer health check) so failures are detected and replaced automatically.
findings.risk: A hung process keeps receiving traffic and is never restarted.
findings.recommendation: Add readiness and liveness probes to containers (or HEALTHCHECK / target group health checks).
findings.example:
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, initialDelaySeconds: 15 }

findings.title: Single-zone data store: aws_db_instance.main
findings.observed: aws_db_instance.main is not configured for multi-AZ failover (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Databases and caches run in more than one availability zone with automatic failover.
findings.risk: A single-zone failure takes the database down until the zone recovers.
findings.recommendation: Enable Multi-AZ (RDS), automatic failover (ElastiCache) or regional availability (Cloud SQL).

findings.title: No record of restore or DR tests
findings.observed: No documentation of backup restore tests or DR exercises was found.
findings.expected: Backup restores are tested on a schedule (quarterly for critical systems), with dated results kept.
findings.risk: Untested backups routinely fail when needed: wrong scope, missing keys, or restores slower than the RTO.
findings.recommendation: Run and record a restore test each quarter: date, what was restored, time taken, and issues found.
findings.example:
## Restore test log
| Date | System | Result | Time | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-30 | Postgres | Pass | 42 min | none |

findings.title: No recovery objectives (RTO/RPO)
findings.observed: No recovery objectives (RTO/RPO) was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: Recovery time and recovery point objectives are defined for each system.
findings.risk: Without objectives, nobody can tell whether backups and failover are adequate until it is too late.
findings.recommendation: Set RTO and RPO per system in the DR plan and design backups and failover to meet them.
findings.example:
| System | RTO | RPO |
|---|---|---|
| API | 1 hour | 15 minutes |

findings.title: No schema validation library
findings.observed: HTTP server or web framework detected in package.json, but no schema validation library (Zod, Joi, Pydantic, validator, ...) is used.
findings.expected: Request bodies, query parameters and webhook payloads are validated server-side with a schema library.
findings.risk: Unvalidated input causes silent data corruption, crashes and injection, and lets clients send totals or IDs the server should compute.
findings.recommendation: Validate every request with a schema (Zod, Pydantic, Joi, validator) and reject what does not match.
findings.example:
const Order = z.object({ sku: z.string().min(1), quantity: z.number().int().positive().max(100) });
const order = Order.parse(req.body);

findings.title: Jobs have no retry limits or dead-letter queue
findings.observed: Job queues are used, but no retry limits, backoff or dead-letter configuration was found.
findings.expected: Jobs and consumers set retry limits with backoff, and failed work lands in a dead-letter queue that is monitored.
findings.risk: Failed jobs are dropped silently or retried forever, losing or duplicating work.
findings.recommendation: Configure attempts and backoff on every queue, and route exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue.
findings.example: await queue.add('send-invoice', data, { attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 } });

findings.title: Schemas declare no integrity constraints
findings.observed: 2 schema or migration file(s) contain no NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign key or check constraints.
findings.expected: Schemas declare NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign key and check constraints, so the database rejects invalid data even when application code misses it.
findings.risk: Without constraints, a single bug writes orphaned or duplicate records that corrupt reports and billing.
findings.recommendation: Declare constraints in the schema for required fields, uniqueness and relationships.

findings.title: No data classification scheme
findings.observed: No data classification scheme was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A classification scheme (e.g. public / internal / confidential / restricted) is defined with handling rules, and applied to data stores and fields.
findings.risk: Without classification, confidential data is handled like everything else: logged, copied to lower environments and shared with vendors.
findings.recommendation: Define classification levels and their handling rules, then tag data stores and sensitive fields.
findings.example:
| Level | Examples | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| Restricted | Card data, credentials | Encrypted fields, no logs, no lower environments |
| Confidential | Customer PII | Encrypted at rest, access logged |

findings.title: Possible real personal data in seeds/customers.json
findings.observed: seeds/customers.json contains 1 valid card number, 1 SSN-shaped value, 1 address at consumer email providers (gmail). Values are not shown.
findings.expected: Seeds, fixtures and sample data are synthetic: test card numbers, reserved example domains, generated identifiers.
findings.risk: Real customer data in the repository is a breach of its own, copied to every clone, CI runner and laptop.
findings.recommendation: Replace real-looking data with synthetic values (example.com addresses, provider test cards) or generate it with Faker; purge any real data from history.

findings.title: No data retention schedule
findings.observed: No data retention schedule was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: Retention periods are defined per data class, and say how data is deleted at the end of them.
findings.risk: Data kept forever is breach exposure without business value, and violates privacy commitments.
findings.recommendation: Document a retention schedule per data class and implement it with TTLs, lifecycle rules or purge jobs.
findings.example:
| Data | Retention | Deletion |
|---|---|---|
| Application logs | 90 days hot, 12 months archive | Bucket lifecycle rule |
| Closed accounts | 30 days | Nightly purge job |

findings.title: No privacy notice in the product
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no privacy notice page or link was found.
findings.expected: A privacy notice is reachable from the product (signup, footer, settings) and describes collection, use, retention, disclosure and disposal.
findings.risk: Collecting personal data without an accessible notice breaches transparency obligations and the SOC 2 privacy commitments.
findings.recommendation: Publish a privacy notice and link it from signup and the site footer; keep prior versions.
findings.example: Privacy notice

findings.title: No personal data map
findings.observed: No personal data map was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A data map lists the personal data collected, where it is stored, why (purpose or legal basis) and for how long.
findings.risk: Without a data map, collection drifts from the privacy notice and access or deletion requests miss data.
findings.recommendation: Keep a data map: each personal data field or category, its purpose, where it is stored, who receives it and its retention.
findings.example:
| Data | Purpose | Stored in | Retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Email | Login, receipts | Postgres users | Account lifetime + 30 days |

findings.title: Sensitive personal data without field-level protection
findings.observed: migrations/002_customers.up.sql defines a sensitive field at line 4, and no field-level encryption or tokenization was found.
findings.expected: Sensitive categories (government IDs, health, biometrics, precise location, date of birth, ...) are encrypted at field level or tokenized, beyond disk encryption.
findings.risk: Sensitive data in plain columns is exposed to every query, backup, replica and analyst with database access.
findings.recommendation: Encrypt sensitive fields at the application layer (envelope encryption with KMS) or tokenize them, and restrict access to the decrypting service.
findings.example: ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN ssn_encrypted bytea;  -- pgp_sym_encrypt with a KMS-managed key

findings.title: No retention purge job or TTL
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no retention purge job or TTL was found in the code.
findings.expected: Personal data past its retention period is removed automatically by scheduled purge jobs, TTL indexes or lifecycle rules.
findings.risk: Without automated deletion, personal data accumulates past its purpose, breaching the privacy notice and enlarging every breach.
findings.recommendation: Add a scheduled job (or TTL index) that deletes or anonymizes personal data once its retention period ends, and alert if it fails.
findings.example:
// nightly
await db.query("DELETE FROM sessions WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days'");

findings.title: No personal data deletion path
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no account deletion, erasure or anonymization code was found.
findings.expected: An account or data deletion path exists (self-service or request-based), and records that are soft-deleted are purged after their retention period.
findings.risk: Without a deletion path, erasure requests cannot be honoured on time; soft deletes that are never purged keep personal data forever.
findings.recommendation: Implement deletion (or irreversible anonymization) for a data subject across all stores, and a scheduled job that purges soft-deleted rows.

findings.title: Soft-deleted records are never purged
findings.observed: Soft deletion is used (migrations/002_customers.up.sql:5), but no job purges soft-deleted rows.
findings.expected: An account or data deletion path exists (self-service or request-based), and records that are soft-deleted are purged after their retention period.
findings.risk: Without a deletion path, erasure requests cannot be honoured on time; soft deletes that are never purged keep personal data forever.
findings.recommendation: Implement deletion (or irreversible anonymization) for a data subject across all stores, and a scheduled job that purges soft-deleted rows.

findings.title: No personal data export path
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no personal data export path was found in the code.
findings.expected: An authenticated export (self-service or support-driven) returns a subject's personal data in a machine-readable format.
findings.risk: Access requests cannot be answered within the legal deadline (often 30 days) without tooling to gather the data.
findings.recommendation: Add an authenticated export that gathers the subject's data from every store into JSON, and track requests with a response deadline.
findings.example: app.get('/me/export', requireAuth, async (req, res) => res.json(await dsar.export(req.user.id)));

findings.title: Undocumented third-party SDKs: Mixpanel
findings.observed: Mixpanel is used but not named in any third-party or privacy document.
findings.expected: Every analytics, advertising, support or session-recording SDK is listed in the third-party or subprocessor inventory, with the data it receives.
findings.risk: Unlisted SDKs collect personal data nobody approved, which the privacy notice then misdescribes.
findings.recommendation: Add each SDK vendor to the third-party inventory (vendor, purpose, data shared), or remove the SDK.
findings.example:
| Vendor | Purpose | Data shared |
|---|---|---|
| PostHog | Product analytics | Pseudonymous user id, page views |

findings.title: Whole user object sent to a third-party SDK
findings.observed: Whole user object sent to a third-party SDK in public/tracking.js at line 8.
findings.expected: Calls to analytics, error-tracking and support SDKs send a pseudonymous id and only the fields the purpose needs, never whole user objects.
findings.risk: Whole user objects leak every field (email, address, flags) to vendors, a rubric red flag and usually a breach of the privacy notice.
findings.recommendation: Send a pseudonymous id and an explicit allow-list of properties.
findings.example:
analytics.identify(user.id, { plan: user.plan });
Sentry.setUser({ id: user.id });

findings.title: No incident and disclosure register
findings.observed: No incident and disclosure register was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: Every detected or reported unauthorized disclosure is recorded with scope, affected subjects, root cause and remediation, and linked to incident response.
findings.risk: Without a register you cannot show regulators or auditors what happened, to whom, and what was fixed.
findings.recommendation: Keep an incident register (a table is enough) and fill it in for every suspected disclosure, even ones that turn out minor.
findings.example:
| Date | Scope | Affected subjects | Root cause | Remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|

findings.title: No breach notification procedure
findings.observed: No breach notification procedure was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A breach procedure sets notification deadlines (e.g. 72 hours to regulators), who is notified (regulators, customers, data subjects), and keeps message templates.
findings.risk: Missing a statutory notification deadline turns an incident into a regulatory violation.
findings.recommendation: Document breach notification deadlines per jurisdiction and contract, who decides, and ready-to-use templates.
findings.example:
## Breach notification
Regulators: within 72 hours of awareness (GDPR Art. 33). Customers: per contract, within 48 hours.
Templates: docs/security/templates/breach-customer.md

findings.title: No privacy contact published
findings.observed: No privacy contact (privacy@ address, DPO or privacy request channel) was found in the docs or the product.
findings.expected: A privacy contact (email or form) is published, and new features handling personal data get a privacy review (the PR template asks about personal data).
findings.risk: Data subjects cannot raise requests or complaints, and features that change data collection ship without review.
findings.recommendation: Publish a privacy contact in the privacy notice and README, and add a personal-data question to the PR template.
findings.example: Privacy questions and requests: privacy@example.com (answered within 30 days).

findings.title: No monitoring defined in code
findings.observed: No error tracking, metrics or dashboard configuration was found in code or IaC.
findings.expected: Error tracking, metrics and dashboards are configured in code (Sentry, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch, ...).
findings.risk: Without instrumentation, security-relevant failures and abuse are invisible until users report them.
findings.recommendation: Instrument the service (error tracking and metrics) and keep dashboards and monitors in code.
findings.example:
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/node';
Sentry.init({ dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN, tracesSampleRate: 0.1 });

findings.title: No SBOM generated
findings.observed: No SBOM tool (Syft, CycloneDX, SPDX, npm sbom) runs in CI.
findings.expected: CI produces an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) for each release or build.
findings.risk: Without an SBOM you cannot answer "are we affected?" quickly when a new vulnerability lands.
findings.recommendation: Generate an SBOM in CI with Syft or a CycloneDX tool and keep it with the release artifacts.
findings.example:
- uses: anchore/sbom-action@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
  with: { format: cyclonedx-json, output-file: sbom.cdx.json }

findings.title: No pull request template
findings.observed: No pull request (or merge request) template was found.
findings.expected: The PR template asks authors to state the security impact of each change.
findings.risk: Without a prompt, security-relevant changes (new endpoints, data flows, dependencies) go through review unflagged.
findings.recommendation: Add a security section with a short checklist to .github/pull_request_template.md.
findings.example:
## Security impact
- [ ] Touches auth, permissions, secrets or personal data
- [ ] Adds a dependency or third-party service
- [ ] Changes infrastructure, network or IAM

findings.title: README does not link security documentation
findings.observed: README.md has no link to SECURITY.md or security documentation.
findings.expected: The README links to the security policy and the security documentation, so people can find them.
findings.risk: Documentation nobody can find is not followed.
findings.recommendation: Add a Security section to the README linking SECURITY.md and your security docs folder.
findings.example:
## Security
See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) to report a vulnerability, and [docs/security](docs/security) for policies and runbooks.

findings.title: No architecture decision records
findings.observed: No ADR directory (docs/adr, decisions/) with decision records was found.
findings.expected: Significant architectural decisions are recorded as ADRs, and ADRs discuss their security considerations.
findings.risk: Without recorded decisions, the security reasoning behind an architecture is lost and gets undone by later changes.
findings.recommendation: Record decisions in docs/adr/NNNN-title.md with a "Security considerations" section.
findings.example:
# 0003. Use OIDC for CI cloud access
## Status
Accepted
## Decision
CI assumes a deploy role through OIDC.
## Security considerations
No long-lived keys in CI; role scoped to the deploy bucket.

findings.title: Dependency and infrastructure changes have no specific reviewer
findings.observed: 4 manifest or IaC file(s) rely on the catch-all owner or none, e.g. Dockerfile, infra/main.tf, legacy/requirements.txt, package.json.
findings.expected: Dependency manifests, Dockerfiles and IaC have specific CODEOWNERS, so adding a dependency, service or datastore is reviewed by someone accountable.
findings.risk: New SDKs and services slip in through routine reviews, bringing data flows and vulnerabilities nobody assessed.
findings.recommendation: Give manifests, Dockerfiles and infrastructure directories specific CODEOWNERS and require code owner review.
findings.example:
/package.json   @your-org/platform
/infra/         @your-org/platform

findings.title: No scheduled security scans
findings.observed: No workflow both runs a security scanner and has a schedule trigger.
findings.expected: Security scans run on a schedule against the default branch, not only on pull requests, so new vulnerabilities in unchanged code are found.
findings.risk: A repository nobody touches is never rescanned, while new CVEs land against its dependencies every week.
findings.recommendation: Add a schedule trigger to the workflow that runs your scanners.
findings.example:
on:
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: '17 6 * * 1'  # weekly

findings.title: No risk-to-control mapping
findings.observed: No risk-to-control mapping was found in the repository's documentation.
findings.expected: A control matrix (or a risk register with a controls column) maps each identified risk to the controls that address it.
findings.risk: Controls that are not tied to risks drift into box-ticking, and uncovered risks go unnoticed.
findings.recommendation: Add a controls column to the risk register, or keep a separate control matrix table.
findings.example:
| Risk | Controls |
|---|---|
| Malicious dependency | Lockfiles, minimumReleaseAge, dependency review |

findings.title: Policy review metadata incomplete: docs/security/old-policy.md
findings.observed: docs/security/old-policy.md: no review date; no owner.
findings.expected: Each policy states its owner and the date it was last reviewed, and is reviewed at least annually.
findings.risk: Stale or ownerless policies describe controls that no longer operate, which auditors test against.
findings.recommendation: Add an owner and a "Last reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD" line to each policy, and review them yearly.
findings.example:
Owner: @security-lead
Last reviewed: 2026-10-01

findings.title: .gitignore does not exclude .env files
findings.observed: .gitignore has no entry matching .env files.
findings.expected: Environment files with real values stay out of version control. Only templates such as .env.example are committed, and .gitignore excludes .env files.
findings.risk: A committed .env file usually holds live credentials, which are then exposed to everyone with repository access and remain in git history.
findings.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.
findings.example:
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

findings.title: Possible literal credential: smtpPassword
findings.observed: `smtpPassword` is assigned a literal value (Hun********) in src/server.js at line 20. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: Credential-like settings read their values from the environment or a secrets manager, never from string literals.
findings.risk: A literal credential in code is shared with everyone who can read the repository and is hard to rotate. This check is heuristic, so confirm each match.
findings.recommendation: Replace the literal with a value loaded at runtime. If it is not a credential, add an exception with a justification.
findings.example:
// After
const client = new Client({ password: process.env.SMTP_PASSWORD });

findings.title: No customer-managed key for aws_db_instance.main
findings.observed: aws_db_instance.main does not set kms_key_id (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Data stores are encrypted with customer-managed KMS keys (with a deletion window), so destroying the key renders all copies, including snapshots, unrecoverable.
findings.risk: With provider-owned keys, decommissioned data and stray snapshots stay readable; disposal relies on finding every copy.
findings.recommendation: Encrypt data stores with a dedicated customer-managed KMS key with rotation enabled.

findings.title: Missing automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate)
findings.observed: No automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) is configured.
findings.expected: Dependabot or Renovate keeps dependencies current, and a vulnerability scan (dependency review, OSV-Scanner, npm audit, pip-audit, govulncheck) runs in CI.
findings.risk: Known-vulnerable dependencies are the most common way attackers get in, and they are only fixed if someone notices.
findings.recommendation: Enable Dependabot (or Renovate) and add a dependency scan to pull-request CI.
findings.example:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }

findings.title: Python requirements not hash-pinned in legacy/requirements.txt
findings.observed: legacy/requirements.txt pins versions but not hashes, so a replaced package would install silently.
findings.expected: Every dependency manifest has a committed lockfile (or hash-pinned requirements) so installs are reproducible.
findings.risk: Without a lockfile, each install can pull different, possibly compromised, versions, and a build cannot be reproduced.
findings.recommendation: Generate the lockfile with your package manager, commit it, and install with the frozen/ci mode in CI.
findings.example:
pnpm install && git add pnpm-lock.yaml       # Node
uv lock && git add uv.lock                    # Python
pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in # pip

findings.title: No infrastructure drift detection
findings.observed: Terraform is used, but no scheduled plan or drift detection was found.
findings.expected: A scheduled `terraform plan` (or a drift detection service) reports changes made outside of code.
findings.risk: Manual console changes silently reopen gaps that code review closed, and are invisible until something breaks.
findings.recommendation: Run `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on a schedule and alert when it reports changes.

findings.title: No documented emergency change process
findings.observed: No document describes an emergency, hotfix or break-glass change process.
findings.expected: An emergency (hotfix / break-glass) change process is documented, including who may use it and the retroactive review it requires.
findings.risk: Without a defined path, urgent fixes bypass review informally and leave no audit trail, which auditors treat as a control failure.
findings.recommendation: Document the emergency change path: who can invoke it, what is skipped, and the retroactive review required within a set time.
findings.example:
## Emergency changes
Use only for active incidents. An on-call engineer may merge with one approval from the incident commander.
A retroactive review PR is opened within 2 business days and linked from the incident ticket.

findings.title: No documented rollback procedure
findings.observed: No runbook or document describing how to roll back a deployment was found.
findings.expected: A runbook explains how to roll back a bad release, who can do it, and how to verify it worked.
findings.risk: Under incident pressure, an undocumented rollback is slow, inconsistent and easy to get wrong.
findings.recommendation: Add a rollback section to your deployment runbook (docs/runbooks/rollback.md) and rehearse it.
findings.example:
## Rolling back a release
1. Find the last good deployment in the Deployments tab.
2. Promote it: `vercel promote <deployment-url>` (or re-run the deploy workflow for the previous tag).
3. Confirm health checks and error rates recover; post in #incidents.

findings.title: No autoscaling or capacity plan
findings.observed: No autoscaling configuration and no documented capacity plan were found.
findings.expected: Workloads autoscale on load, or a documented capacity plan sets headroom targets.
findings.risk: Traffic spikes (or abuse) exhaust fixed capacity and cause an outage.
findings.recommendation: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler or cloud autoscaling policy, or document a capacity plan with headroom targets.

findings.title: No load tests
findings.observed: The repository serves HTTP but has no load or performance tests.
findings.expected: Load tests (k6, Artillery, Locust, Gatling, ...) exist and run before major releases.
findings.risk: Capacity limits are discovered in production, during the busiest hour.
findings.recommendation: Add a load test for the critical paths and run it before major releases.

findings.title: No API contract
findings.observed: The repository serves an API but has no OpenAPI, GraphQL or protobuf contract.
findings.expected: The API has a machine-readable contract (OpenAPI, GraphQL schema, protobuf) kept in the repository or generated from code.
findings.risk: Without a contract, clients and the service disagree about inputs and outputs, and breaking changes go unnoticed.
findings.recommendation: Commit an OpenAPI document (or GraphQL schema / .proto files), or generate one from code, and version it.

findings.title: No changelog
findings.observed: No CHANGELOG, CHANGES, HISTORY or release notes file at the repository root.
findings.expected: A changelog or release notes record each version, including breaking changes.
findings.risk: Users and downstream systems are surprised by breaking changes, causing processing errors.
findings.recommendation: Keep a CHANGELOG.md (Keep a Changelog format) and call out breaking changes explicitly.
findings.example:
## 2.0.0
### Breaking
- `/v1/orders` removed; use `/v2/orders`.

findings.title: No lifecycle rule for aws_s3_bucket.exports
findings.observed: aws_s3_bucket.exports has no lifecycle configuration, so objects are kept forever (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Buckets have lifecycle expiration, log groups have a retention period, and ephemeral tables use TTLs.
findings.risk: Without automated deletion, data (and logs full of it) accumulates forever, enlarging every breach.
findings.recommendation: Add lifecycle expiration to buckets and retention_in_days to log groups, matching your retention schedule.

findings.title: No profile or account update path
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no profile or account update path was found in the code.
findings.expected: Users can update their own personal data (profile or account settings), or request correction through support tooling.
findings.risk: Inaccurate personal data cannot be corrected on request, and errors propagate to downstream systems.
findings.recommendation: Provide an authenticated profile update (with validation and an audit trail) and propagate changes to downstream systems.
findings.example: app.patch('/me', requireAuth, async (req, res) => res.json(await users.update(req.user.id, ProfileSchema.parse(req.body))));

findings.title: No intake for vendor breach notices
findings.observed: No document describes how breach or incident notices from vendors and subprocessors are received and handled.
findings.expected: There is a documented intake for breach or incident notices from vendors and subprocessors, routed into incident response.
findings.risk: A vendor's breach notice sent to an unmonitored inbox starts your own notification clock without anyone knowing.
findings.recommendation: Name the address vendors must notify, who monitors it, and that notices open an incident.
findings.example:
## Vendor incident notices
Subprocessors notify security@example.com within 48 hours (per the DPA). Each notice opens an incident and is triaged as SEV2 or higher.

findings.title: No validation of personal data fields
findings.observed: The application stores personal data (e.g. migrations/001_init.up.sql:1), but no validation of personal data fields was found in the code.
findings.expected: Personal data fields are validated for format and completeness (e.g. email and phone formats) when collected.
findings.risk: Malformed contact data makes notification, access and deletion requests fail to reach or match the right person.
findings.recommendation: Validate personal data at the boundary with a schema (email, phone, dates) and normalize before storing.
findings.example: const Signup = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), name: z.string().min(1).max(200) });

findings.title: No privacy review in the change process
findings.observed: Neither the PR template nor a PIA/DPIA process asks about personal data.
findings.expected: A privacy contact (email or form) is published, and new features handling personal data get a privacy review (the PR template asks about personal data).
findings.risk: Data subjects cannot raise requests or complaints, and features that change data collection ship without review.
findings.recommendation: Publish a privacy contact in the privacy notice and README, and add a personal-data question to the PR template.
findings.example: Privacy questions and requests: privacy@example.com (answered within 30 days).
